passage: During PE at the sports club's junior session, Ritu tripped over the cone and skidded on her knees. Her friend Kalyani was next to her in a second. The coach was on the far side. Ritu's face crumpled but she did not cry. Kalyani put a hand on her back and said, "Take a breath. I'm here." Ritu nodded. "Does it look bad?" Kalyani checked. "There's a scrape. It's not bleeding much, but let's go to Coach." She didn't say "it's nothing". She walked beside Ritu, holding her water bottle, and waited outside the first-aid room until Ritu came out with a plaster on her knee.

qa.q: What did Ritu trip over?
qa.a: She tripped over the cone.

qa.q: What was Ritu probably feeling when her face crumpled but she did not cry, and what did Kalyani do about it?
qa.a: She was probably in pain and upset, and maybe embarrassed. Kalyani stayed close, kept calm and told her honestly about the scrape.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do next if Ritu is still shaky?
qa.a: She can keep walking with her, ask what she needs, and avoid empty promises like saying it is nothing.

qa.q: How might the coach see Kalyani's help?
qa.a: The coach, far away, would see a friend who reached Ritu quickly and brought her to first aid.

grounding: A child stays close after a friend's fall and says it is okay only truthfully, showing reassurance that matches the friend's need.

passage: I was on the bench at the community centre when Jatin's little brother's kite string cut Amandeep's palm during the kite race. Amandeep looked at his hand and then at the ground. Jatin dropped his own kite and stood beside him, saying, "It'll be okay, it won't hurt anymore." Amandeep frowned and shook his head. Jatin stopped, thought, and said, "Sorry, it probably does hurt. Do you want me to get someone?" Amandeep nodded. Jatin ran to the volunteer while I watched. When he came back, he stayed next to Amandeep and said nothing else. I couldn't tell if Amandeep was more hurt or embarrassed.

qa.q: What cut Amandeep's palm?
qa.a: Jatin's little brother's kite string cut Amandeep's palm.

qa.q: What might Amandeep's frown and headshake have meant about what he wanted, and what else could explain them?
qa.a: He probably felt it did hurt and wanted honest help, not a promise. It could also be that he was embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Jatin do when a friend is hurt and his first words don't match?
qa.a: He can adjust, as he did, by admitting it probably hurts and offering help, then stay near without more promises.

qa.q: How might the observer see Jatin's change of words?
qa.a: The observer sees a child notice a friend's frown and change course. She stays unsure what Amandeep truly felt.

grounding: A child pats a friend and stays close after a fall, and learns reassurance works when it matches the friend's need, avoiding empty promises.

passage:
Monday: Siddharth fell off his cycle outside the society gate and scraped his knee. Tanvir ran over. "It's nothing, it's fine, you're okay!" Siddharth looked at the blood and cried harder.
Wednesday: Siddharth didn't want to ride again. "What if I fall?" Tanvir almost said "you won't fall," but stopped. That wasn't true, and Siddharth knew it.
Instead he said, "Maybe you will. But I'll run next to you, holding the seat, till you say let go."
Friday: They practised in the parking lot. Tanvir jogged beside him, puffing. After three rounds, Siddharth said, "Let go." He wobbled, then rode all the way to the gate. He looked back and grinned.

qa.q: What did Tanvir say on Monday when Siddharth fell?
qa.a: "It's nothing, it's fine, you're okay!"

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he asked "What if I fall?"
qa.a: Siddharth felt scared and nervous about getting hurt again after Monday's fall.

qa.q: What changed in Tanvir's way of reassuring?
qa.a: He stopped giving an empty promise and offered something real that matched the need, running beside Siddharth holding the seat. 👍

qa.q: What would change if Tanvir had said "you won't fall"?
qa.a: Siddharth might not believe him, and if he did fall again, he might trust Tanvir's comfort less.

grounding: Over several days, a child learns that reassurance works when it matches a friend's need, not with empty promises.

passage:
"Lalit, you told Rishi his mother wouldn't be angry about the broken vase? Hmm. Let me, your Jeevan Dadu, tell you something.
When I was in Class 5, in Nashik, my friend Ganesh fell during the school race and tore his only uniform shirt. He was crying, scared of the headmaster. I patted his back and said, 'Don't worry, Sir won't even notice.'
But Sir did notice. He scolded Ganesh in front of everyone. Ganesh looked at me as if I had lied to him.
After that I learned. Now I say, 'I'll come with you,' or 'Let's tell him together.' Not promises I can't keep."

qa.q: What did Ganesh tear during the school race?
qa.a: His only uniform shirt.

qa.q: What was young Jeevan feeling when Ganesh looked at him after the scolding?
qa.a: Jeevan felt guilty and ashamed, because his comfort had turned out to be an empty promise.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could have matched Ganesh's need better?
qa.a: Jeevan could have offered to go with Ganesh to the headmaster instead of promising Sir wouldn't notice.

qa.q: How might Ganesh have felt when he was scolded after Jeevan's promise?
qa.a: Ganesh probably felt hurt and let down, as if his friend had tricked him.

grounding: A grandfather recalls giving an empty promise to reassure a friend and learning to match comfort to the real need.

passage:
The football match was in pouring rain, and the coach was on the far side of the field. Jeevan slipped in the mud and twisted his ankle. He sat, holding it, face white.
Darshan ran over and crouched beside him. He didn't say "it's nothing" or "you'll be fine." He could see it hurt.
"I'll stay right here," Darshan said. "Coach is coming. Do you want to hold my arm?"
Jeevan grabbed his arm tight. Rain dripped off his nose.
"I'm scared I broke it," Jeevan whispered.
"I don't know," Darshan said honestly. "But I'm not leaving."
When the coach arrived, Darshan helped lift Jeevan onto the bench, still holding his arm.

qa.q: What did Darshan offer Jeevan to hold?
qa.a: His arm.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he whispered about his ankle?
qa.a: Jeevan felt scared and worried that he had broken it.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that matched Jeevan's need?
qa.a: He stayed close, told the truth instead of an empty promise, and offered his arm until the coach came.

qa.q: How might the coach see Darshan's help?
qa.a: The coach would likely be grateful that Darshan stayed calm and kept Jeevan company in the rain.

grounding: In a rainy match, a child reassures an injured friend by staying close and avoiding empty promises.

passage: Mridul's skate caught a crack in the colony road and he went down hard, palms first. Ira skidded to a stop and knelt beside him. His hands were scraped and his eyes were full. Ira nearly said, "It's nothing, get up," but she saw his chin shaking. Instead she patted his shoulder. "That was a big fall. I'm staying right here." Mridul sniffed. "Mummy will be so angry. I broke the rule about the main road." Ira wanted to say, "She won't be," but she didn't know that. "I'll come with you when you tell her," she said. They walked home slowly, Ira carrying both pairs of skates. Mridul's mummy washed his palms first and talked about the rule afterwards.

qa.q: What did Mridul's skate catch?
qa.a: A crack in the colony road.

qa.q: Why did Ira hold back from saying "She won't be"?
qa.a: Ira felt caring but wanted to stay honest, and didn't want to make an empty promise about something she couldn't know.

qa.q: Which of Ira's words matched what Mridul needed?
qa.a: Naming the big fall, staying close, and offering to come along when he told Mummy, instead of 'it's nothing' or a promise she couldn't keep 🙂

qa.q: What was the fall like for Mridul?
qa.a: Painful and scary, with scraped palms and a shaking chin, plus worry that Mummy would be angry about the rule.

grounding: It shows a child reassuring a friend after a fall by staying close and matching words to the friend's need, while avoiding an empty promise.
